technique: repetition with a difference — a word or shape returning changed
lesson:
Today we work on one move: repetition with a difference. That means a word or a shape comes back, but changed the second time.

Watch for the pairs in this poem. First, "a yes you can lean your whole weight on, a no that holds." Same sentence shape, two opposite words. Then earlier, "the full sack from the hollow, the sound board from the split." Again, two things set against each other in the same frame.

Here is why that works on you. When you hear the shape a second time, you expect it, so your ear relaxes. Then the word inside is different, so you pay attention to the change. The repeated shape holds the two things close enough to compare.

Try this: write one line with two parts that match in rhythm but name opposite things, like "a door that opens, a wall that stays."

The second time through, count how many times a pair shows up before "So — up!" comes.

Here is the poem.
poem:
The handle of the cold-shed door has worn to fit you,
that one smooth dent where your thumb has learned its place,
and you take it the way you take most things now—
by feel, before the eyes are much good for anything.
Out here a man can tell the true from the false by hand:
the full sack from the hollow, the sound board from the split,
the clean pull of a latch that's been kept honest.
Something in you wants the world to answer plain like that—
a yes you can lean your whole weight on, a no that holds.
The ridge is going gray to silver, the frost laid down like salt,
and the cold comes clean into your chest and wakes you all the way.

The light's already doing its quiet work out there, and the day's got a few small things waiting that only your hands can finish—

So — up!
